# Telecom Support

`customer_support.model.b2b.telecom` · vertical · parent `customer_support.model.b2b`

> Supporting business connectivity and voice services. This is the vertical where support process is industrialised, and the three consequences are unusually concrete. The SLA is an invoice. Availability and restoration targets carry contractual service credits that are computed from clock data and paid out, so clock accuracy is an accounting control rather than a reporting nicety. A pause applied incorrectly is not a dashboard artefact; it is a billing dispute the customer's procurement team will pursue, and a breach we failed to self-declare is worse than the outage that caused it. Most faults are not on our equipment. The path runs across last-mile access we resell, peering we do not own, and customer premises equipment nobody has looked at in four years. The actual craft is sectionalisation — proving which segment is at fault before committing an engineer — and it is slow, adversarial and mostly conducted against other carriers who have their own trouble-ticket process and their own clocks that do not align with ours. Planned work is a different object from a fault. A degradation inside a notified maintenance window is contractually not an outage, and a customer reporting one has usually not read the notice — which makes proactive notification a support function with commercial consequences rather than an operations courtesy. The error carried in from SaaS is treating the SLA as a service standard we set for ourselves and can miss with an apology. The error carried in from hardware is assuming we can dispatch our way out; here the engineer frequently has to be someone else's.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | a network or IT manager at the customer, often reading the same alarms we are, and frequently already on a bridge with their own users waiting |
| typical_resolution_hours | 8 |
| volume_shape | steady trouble-ticket baseline with hard correlated spikes on any core, access or upstream event; a single fibre cut generates a synchronised wave |
| staffing_model | NOC-fronted with tiered field and core engineering, formal shift handover, and carrier-to-carrier escalation paths |
| coverage | 24x7 by construction — the network does not observe business hours and neither can the fault desk |
| automation_level | high on detection and correlation, low on customer resolution — alarms self-raise tickets long before anyone can explain them |
| notes | Detection automation without correlation is a known failure here: one fibre cut can auto-raise hundreds of tickets, and a queue that treats them as hundreds of problems has already lost the outage.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.sla_target`

Requires `clock_state`, `exclusions`, `credit_exposure`, `is_contractual`


> Credit exposure has to be visible on the live clock, not computed at month end, because it is what makes prioritisation rational under load — two breaching tickets with different credit consequences are not equally urgent. Exclusions are mandatory for the same reason: maintenance windows and force-majeure carve-outs are the difference between a breach and a non-event, and they are agreed in the contract, not decided at triage.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.incident`

Requires `declared_at`, `broadcast_cadence_minutes`, `affected_account_count`, `comms_owner_ref`


> A named communications owner separate from the incident commander is standard here for a reason: the commander is on the technical bridge and cannot also be writing customer updates on a fixed cadence, and when one person tries to do both, the updates stop exactly when the customers most need them.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `severity`, `product_area_ref`, `escalation_ref`


> Product area here means network segment, and it is what allows a hundred tickets to collapse into one fault. A ticket without it is a customer complaint with no path to the cause, which is precisely what an alarm-generated queue fills up with.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> typical_resolution_hours of 8 is a median across a bimodal queue — configuration and voice faults close in an hour, physical access faults take days waiting on a third-party engineer. The bimodality is the point and averaging it away is how this vertical gets mis-staffed.
